titleStmt.title: SysMix: Mixed-Size Placement for Systolic-Array-Based Hierarchical Designs

analytic.title: SysMix: Mixed-Size Placement for Systolic-Array-Based Hierarchical Designs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Systolic array designs are gaining popularity due to their applications in hardware acceleration for ML computing, such as CNNs and transformers. Increasingly large ML models necessitate very high circuit energy-efficiency, which is highly correlated with minimizing placement wirelength in chip physical design. However, existing placement techniques are mostly general purpose and overlook unique properties of systolic array designs. We propose a mixed-size placement approach, called SysMix, which is tailored for systolic arrays and leverage their partial regularity in hierarchical design methodologies. Experimental results from multiple CNN designs show that SysMix achieves 53% wirelength reduction and 15X speedup compared to a commercial placer and a state-of-the-art academic placer.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Systolic array, composed of an array of PEs (Processing Elements), serves as a cornerstone for massively parallel computing. Systolic arrays are popular in hardware acceleration for ML (Machine Learning) computing, such as CNNs (Convolutional Neural Networks) and transformers, and have been adopted in industry, e.g., Google TPU [11]. As shown in Figure 1, systolic arrays are characterized by their highly regular structure, coupled with interconnect dominated by local connections, i.e., connections between adjacent PEs as opposed to non-adjacent PEs. Intuitively, such a regular structure is very friendly to layout designs and can potentially facilitate improved layout solution quality. Since all PEs in a systolic array are identical, they can be pre-designed as hard IP blocks, a.k.a. macros. Such macro IP-based design reuse is commonly seen in hierarchical design methodologies and SoC designs. At the same time, the control logic circuit does not exhibit such a regular structure and is distributed throughout the array. Therefore, it can be regarded as a set of dust cells. We will present a mixed-size placement approach for such systolic array designs in hierarchical design methodologies. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first study on mixed-size placement tailored for systolic array designs on ASICs (Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) by leveraging their regularity. Although mixed-size placement has been extensively studied in the past [3,6,15,1,4], they are mostly general-purpose and pay almost no attention to design regularities. Design regularity is considered in datapath placement [7,20]. In addition to the difference between systolic array's 2D regularity and conventional datapath's 1D regularity, dust cells exist between PEs of a systolic array while datapath cells form contiguous rows without random logic cells in the middle. Therefore, datapath placement techniques are not directly applicable to systolic array designs. A macro placement approach for TPU designs is introduced in [19]. It is a reinforcement learning approach with little emphasis on exploiting the design regularity. Systolic array placement is also studied for FPGAs (Field-Programmable Gate Arrays) [14,10].

Although the work of [9] is for placement of systolic array designs, it treats all PE cells as dust cells and solves a cell placement problem instead of mixed-size placement. Thus, it is for flat designs as opposed to hierarchical designs as in our work. Both flat design and hierarchical design are popular methodologies, and each has its own advantages and disadvantages. In a hierarchical design methodology, where the PE design is purchased from an IP vendor, it makes little business sense to flatten the PE design and use cell placement like [9]. Likewise, in a flat design methodology, it is usually better to apply cell placement like [9] than macro-based mixed-size placement like our work. Therefore, the work of [9] and ours are designed for two different application scenarios and not directly comparable.

The exploitation of structural regularity in placement of systolic array designs is not as straightforward as it appears to be. Due to the PE connections with global buffer, control logic cells, and IO pins, placing PEs in a strictly regular array usually results in increased wirelength. Instead, small wirelength results often exhibit partial regularity, where the spatial orders among PEs generally follow the schematic but there is not necessarily alignment for rows and columns. To solve the problem of mixed-size placement with partial regularity, we propose SysMix, an approach with three key ingredients: (1) PE-driven dust cell clustering; (2) regularityaware macro/PE placement via LP (Linear Programming); (3) dust cell placement with a new initial placement technique. In SysMix, the regularity is exploited to reduce solution search space and help achieve better solution quality. The benefits of exploiting the regularity are clearly observed in the experimental results. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows.
• This is the first study on exploiting regularity for mixed-size placement of systolic arrays in hierarchical designs, to the best of our knowledge.

div.head: PREVIOUS WORKS
div.p: Mixed-size Placement. NTUplace3 [3] is an early influential work on mixed-size placement based on multi-level analytical techniques. RePlAce [6] is an electrostatics-based analytical placer, which outperforms most of its prior works on public domain benchmark suites and forms the key basis for many recent placers. DREAMPlace [15] is a very fast analytical placer leveraging neural network training infrastructure and GPUs. AutoDMP [1] is a mixed-size placement framework based on DREAMPlace. It uses multi-objective Bayesian optimization to fine-tune the parameters of the DREAMPlace engine, and achieves PPA (Performance, Power, Area) comparable to commercial tools. The work of [4] proposes a stronger mixed-size global placement backbone based on DREAMPlace. It archives better robustness for convergence, and better HPWL (Half-Perimeter Wire-Length) and PPA.

Macro Placement. Macro placement has been extensively studied, and we summarize some recent research results in this area. MDP-trees [16] is a simulated annealing-based macro placement approach, where the MDP (Multi-Domain Packing) tree is a new solution representation technique. A deep reinforcement learning-based macro placement approach is presented in [19] and has been applied in Google TPU designs. RTL-MP [12] is a simulated annealing-based macro placer that exploits RTL information regarding logical hierarchy. It achieves equally good or better PPA than a commercial tool and human experts, but suffers from scalability in runtime. A comparative study on different macro placement and mixed-size placement methods is provided in [5]. The results show that routed wirelength, area, and power are often highly correlated. AutoDMP and a commercial tool often achieve the best results in this study.

Datapath Placement. In [7], datapath cells are first clustered into a single macro and then a mixed-size placement is performed. Next, the datapath macro is declustered and datapath cells are placed while the random logic cells are fixed. It concludes with a random logic placement fine-tuning stage. The work of [20] simultaneously places datapath cells and random logic cells through a force-directed algorithm. Pseudo nets are inserted to align cells across multiple-bit slices to address datapath regularity.

Systolic Array Design Placement. In [14], a simulated annealing-based FPGA placement technique is developed considering the 2D regularity of systolic arrays. It achieves a 2X to 28X speedup compared to VPR [17], a well-known FPGA layout tool, with limited circuit performance loss. The work of [9] proposes a global placement framework using soft 2D regularity constraints for systolic array-based CNN designs. It places PE cells instead of PE macros in flat design methodologies. Compared with RePlAce, it reduces HPWL by 6%. Since flat designs have fewer constraints than hierarchical designs, they may lead to better solution quality at the expense of longer turn-around time. Although it is also a systolic array placer, comparing a mixed-size placement and a cell placement of the same circuit would mostly disclose the difference between a hierarchical design methodology versus a flat design methodology instead of the effectiveness of placement algorithms. A new algorithmic approach for systolic array placement on FPGAs is proposed in [10]. Compared with other FPGA placement tools, it obtains a 24% reduction in HPWL.
Summary. There is almost no prior study on mixed-size placement for systolic array designs in ASICs by leveraging their regularity.

div.head: BACKGROUND 3.1 Graph Clustering by Bubble-FOS/C
div.p: We make use of Bubble-FOS/C [18], a graph partitioning/clustering algorithm, in our mixed-size placement. It is a connectivity-driven approach rather than minimizing cut sizes. Its framework has three stages: (1) randomly choosing a certain number of nodes as seeds;

(2) growing each cluster from a seed node to its neighboring nodes by simulating fluid diffusion till all nodes are clustered; (3) for each cluster, finding its center as the new seed and regrowing from the new seeds to form new clusters. In our work, only stage 2 is needed as the seeds are PEs, which do not need to be randomly selected at the beginning or reselected after stage 2. Stage 2 is an iterative process. In each iteration, a certain amount of fluid moves from node 𝑣 𝑗 to another 𝑣 𝑖 with probability 𝐴 𝑖,𝑗 if there is an edge (𝑣 𝑖 , 𝑣 𝑗 ) in the given graph. The probability depends on the connectivity between 𝑣 𝑖 and 𝑣 𝑗 . At the end, a node is assigned to a cluster if its fluid mostly comes from the seed of this cluster. This iterative simulation of diffusion behaves like a Markov chain, and probabilities 𝐴 𝑖,𝑗 can be treated as state transition probabilities of the Markov chain.

div.head: PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: The input is a systolic array-based design characterized by a hypergraph 𝐺 = (𝑉 , 𝐸). The node set 𝑉 is composed of a set of PEs 𝑃, a set of dust cells 𝐶 and a set of fixed pins 𝑇 corresponding to IOs and preplaced global buffer, i.e., 𝑉 = 𝑃 ∪ 𝐶 ∪ 𝑇 . Set 𝑃 is an 𝑀 × 𝐾 array of PEs, where 𝑀 and 𝐾 are natural numbers. The hyperedge set 𝐸 is the netlist indicating connections among PEs, dust cells, and fixed pins. Each PE is treated as a hard macro, and its internal nets are neglected. The mixed-size placement is to decide PE and dust cell locations in a 2D plane such that the total HPWL (Half Perimeter Wire-Length) is minimized and there is no overlap among any PEs, dust cells, and fixed pins. Mixed-size placement for systolic array designs exploiting regularity is a relatively new problem. As such, it will be tackled in a step-by-step manner with an emphasis on HPWL in this work like many other mixed-size placement works. Other objectives, such as routability, will be addressed in our future research.

div.head: THE PROPOSED SYSMIX PLACEMENT 5.1 Overview
div.p: Although the structure of a systolic array is very regular, its placement is not straightforward for two reasons. First, there are wire connections between PEs and fixed pins, which may distort the regularity. Second, there are a significant number of dust cells interleaved between PEs, which also disturb the regularity. The effect of fixed pins and dust cells on regularity is demonstrated in [9]. Such partial regularity is significantly more difficult to exploit than complete regularity. A similar difficulty is also observed in datapath placement [20]. On the other hand, even partial regularity provides an opportunity for further HPWL reduction. An overview of our proposed SysMix placement methodology is provided in Figure 2. In the phase of macro placement, PEs are placed with the consideration of dust cells through dust cell clustering. The macro placement is realized through LP. In the second phase, dust cells are placed while the PEs are fixed. Both the macro placement and dust cell placement leverage the partial regularity of systolic array designs.

div.head: Dust Cell
div.p: Clustering for C3-Macro Generation. A C3-macro consists of a PE surrounded by a subset of related dust cells, like a Chocolate-Covered Cherry. The PE is a hard macro (cherry) and its surrounding dust cells form a firm shell (chocolate). In this step, every dust cell is clustered to a certain PE to form an 𝑀 × 𝐾 array of C3-macros. Such C3-macros provide a rough estimate of how much space to be reserved for dust cells around each PE when deciding PE locations. This is a special graph clustering problem different from ordinary graph clustering/partitioning [2,13]. Thus, we adopt the Bubble-FOS/C algorithm [18], which fits our need very well. The overall Bubble-FOS/C algorithm is briefly reviewed in Section 3.1. Since we can directly use PEs as cluster seeds and there is no need for further seed adjustment, only stage 2 of Bubble-FOS/C is employed here.

div.head: Dust Cell Placement
div.p: In this phase, dust cells are declustered from C3-macros and placed while the PE locations are fixed. Our dust cell placement includes three steps: (1) initial placement; (2) global placement; (3) detailed placement and legalization. The initial placement in our SysMix is a new technique that makes use of the regularity of systolic arrays and will be elaborated later in this section. The global placement is carried out using RePlAce [6] with a change. Although PE areas intuitively need to be counted toward cell densities in global placement, their large sizes overshadow the density of dust cells, which are to be placed in this phase. In order to let RePlAce focus on dust cells instead of PEs, we scale PE dimensions with a factor the same as the target density throughout our execution of RePlAce-based dust cell placement. Step 3, detailed placement and legalization, is realized by calling NTUplace3 [3].

In conventional cell placement methods [3,6], initial solutions are generated randomly or through quadratic placement. In our SysMix, we propose a new initial solution technique for dust cells by leveraging the regularity of systolic array designs. The main idea is to use the PE placement as a backbone and then place dust cells using the results of clustering described in Section 5.2.1.

The initial placement is based on dust cell connections with PEs. For simplicity, we use cells to refer dust cells. The netlist connections are described by matrix 𝐴, which is described in Section 5. The process for generating the cell-PE connection matrix Φ is outlined in Algorithm 1. Lines 10-14 examine the upper-right sub-matrix of 𝐴 to account for the direct connections in Φ. div.head: Experiment Setup
div.p: Several systolic array-based CNN circuit designs are obtained according to [21] for ASIC style. These circuits are synthesized using Synopsys Design Compiler with the ASAP7 cell library [8]. They cover different dataflow types, WS (Weight Stationary) and OS (Output Stationary), and various PE array sizes. The characteristics of these circuits are summarized in the first column of Table 1.
We compared our method (SysMix) with the following state-ofthe-art mixed-size placers
• RePlAce [6];
• DREAMPlace [15];
• AutoDMP [1];
• The work of [4];
• A commercial placement tool.

AutoDMP usually generates multiple solutions with different PPA (Performance Power Area) tradeoffs. We pick its minimum HPWL solution for a fair comparison. Except AutoDMP and [4], all the other methods are evaluated on an 8-thread CPU machine with 3.4GHz frequency and 250GB RAM. AutoDMP can only be performed on a GPU platform, and it runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 Ti in this experiment. The result of [4] was obtained from an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 GPU.

div.head: Main Results
div.p: The main results of HPWL and total runtime are summarized in Table 1. All the HPWL values except those labeled with illegal are legalized results. For those results labeled with illegal, global placement was successful, and their global placement HPWL results are reported if available. Please note that each tool has its own legalizer, e.g., the legalization of DREAMPlace was performed using DREAMPlace's legalizer. The global placement of RePlAce cannot converge for circuit WS8 and circuit WS64. Among the six methods being compared, only our SysMix, the commercial tool, and AutoDMP can successfully find legalized solutions for all circuits. Compared to the commercial tool and Au-toDMP, our SysMix can reduce wirelength by over 53% on average and are 15× -217× faster. Although DREAMPlace's results look close to ours, DREAMPlace failed to legalize five out of the eight circuits. Among all methods, RePlAce is the fastest, but it failed in three circuits, and the available HPWL results are 78% larger than our SysMix on average. The method of [4] failed in legalizing WS32 and generated 2.7× HPWL compared to our SysMix. (1) Regular PE placement. PEs instead of C3-macros are placed in a regular 2D array, where rows and columns are well aligned. Then, dust cells are placed using RePlAce with the PEs are fixed. This approach is straightforward yet the tricky part is the spacing among adjacement PEs. Since this is a regular array, the spacing for different columns and rows are the same. Too small spacing may cause legalization failures while too large spacing increases HPWL unnecessarily. For each case, we conduct multiple runs and choose the minimum spacing that allows successful legalization. (2) RePlAce with regular initial PE placement (RePlAce-RI). This is almost the same as RePlAce except that the initial PE placement is a regular 2D array instead of a random placement. Since this is merely an initial solution, the spacing among rows and columns is not important. The comparison results are shown in Table 2. Compared to the regular PE placement, SysMix can reduce legalized HPWL by almost a half and decrease runtime by 15%. This shows that the impact of dust cells and IO pins is complicated and cannot be handled by a very regular PE layout. RePlAce-RI shows much better results than the RePlAce results, which are shown in Table 1. However, it still causes 20% higher HPWL, which is quite significant for placement. Moreover, RePlAce cannot yet converge for WS8, even with the regular initial solution. Compared to random initial placement, our method reduces HPWL and global placement runtime by 6% and 33%, respectively. Compared to QP-based initial placement, our initial placement leads to 3% smaller HPWL and 30% reduction of the total runtime of initial placement and global placement. Since our initial solutions are computed very quickly and make dust cells well located, the remaining RePlAce iterations can be significantly reduced. 3. Compared to the naïve clustering, the Bubble-FOS/C-based clustering in our method leads to 30% reduction in HPWL and 25% total placement runtime reduction. One reason for this difference is that Bubble-FOS/C clustering is based on a relatively sophisticated connectivity metric of Equation (5), which reflects the effect of net degrees. In addition, diffusion is a natural way to capture this metric through multiple connecting paths between dust cells and PEs. There are two parameters for the dust cell clustering described in Section 5.2.1. One is the diagonal element value 𝑔 for the connectivity matrix 𝐴, and the other is the number of iterations. We evaluate the impact of these parameters on case WS8. Since the impact on total runtime is limited, we mainly focus on the legalized HPWL, which is depicted in Figure 8. One can see that too few iterations increase HPWL. When the number of iterations is sufficiently large, the middle choice of diagonal values 𝑔 leads to the best HPWL. This is consistent with our expectation that 𝑔 should not be too large or too small.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH
div.p: This work provides the first study on mixed-size placement for systolic array designs in hierarchical ASIC style, to the best of our knowledge. The proposed approach SysMix makes use of partial regularity in systolic array designs and produces significantly better wirelength results compared to state-of-the-art techniques including a commercial tool, which either fail in obtaining legalized solutions or lead to considerably greater wirelength. Ablation studies have been performed to the effectiveness of each component in our SysMix placer. In future research, we will extend this work to handle routability and evaluate solutions with global routing.

figure.figDesc: Figure 7: Global placement runtime and total (global+initial) placement runtime.6.3.3 Effectiveness of Dust CellClustering. We compared our placer using the Bubble-FOS/C clustering (Section 5.2.1) with a naïve dust cell clustering method embedded in our placement framework. In this naïve clustering, a dust cell is clustered to its nearest neighbor PE according to the number of hops in the circuit graph. The comparison results are shown in Table3. Compared to the naïve clustering, the Bubble-FOS/C-based clustering in our method leads to 30% reduction in HPWL and 25% total placement runtime reduction. One reason for this difference is that Bubble-FOS/C clustering is based on a relatively sophisticated connectivity metric of Equation(5), which reflects the effect of net degrees. In addition, diffusion is a natural way to capture this metric through multiple connecting paths between dust cells and PEs.

When PEs are not scaled as such, the global placement fails to converge for both WS8 and OS8, the two smallest cases.
